#9689. Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9688. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

#9687. Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

Dark Reading Confidential Episode 23: Cyber insurers share their view of the AI-driven threat landscape and how mounting challenges are putting pressure on both sides of the policy, leaving the current model unsustainable.

Cyber insurance providers are approaching 2027 facing a fundamental challenge. Claims rose 40% in 2024 and another 20% in 2025, even as premiums have stayed largely flat. This trend is something both Coalition and Travelers say isn't sustainable; and at the center of that shift is AI, which is reshaping the threat landscape not by inventing new attack types, but by making existing ones — ransomware, business email compromise, and phishing — dramatically easier to execute at scale.

In this episode of Dark Reading Confidential, Dark Reading media and projects director Becky Bracken and Dark Reading senior news director Rob Wright sit down with Lauren Winchester, vice president of cyber-risk services at Travelers; and Daniel Woods, head of emerging risk at Coalition, to unpack what the data actually shows. The conversation moves past the headline-grabbing surge in disclosed vulnerabilities to a more nuanced picture: exploitation is rising, but not as sharply as disclosure volume, while AI-powered phishing kits are bring sold SaaS-style to criminals with little technical skill, driving a measurable spike in BEC and ransomware activity.

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

The two insurers also agree on where the real exposure lies: not necessarily with large enterprises, which have the resources to track threat intelligence and patch quickly, but with small and mid-sized businesses that often lack an in-house IT team altogether. That awareness gap, they argue, is where insurers now have to step in — not just to underwrite risk, but to actively help policyholders defend their organizations against it.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please listen to the podcast or watch the video.

Dark Reading's Becky Bracken: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Dark Reading Confidential, a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, where we bring you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. My name is Becky Bracken. I'm an editor with Dark Reading, and I am thrilled today to do just that: deliver as promised, along with my colleague Rob Wright. Today we are going to be talking about all things cyber insurance and AI. In addition to my very smart colleague Rob Wright, who I mentioned, we are thrilled to welcome Lauren Winchester, who is vice president of cyber risk services at Travelers Insurance, and of course Daniel Woods, who is the head of emerging risk at Coalition. Welcome to both of you. Thank you.

So, I am going to get out of the way and let Rob explain some of his very smart thinking around this topic, and get you guys in on it.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: It wasn't a smart idea, but it was a question about what is happening with cyber insurance now that we have all this AI stuff going on. Thank you for joining me on this. We'll start with a basic question about where the cyber insurance industry is right now today in 2026, going into 2027. Just broad strokes. I know it's still somewhat of a new market, but where do you feel like it is in terms of overall health and growth? Daniel, why don't you kick us off?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So I think the best data source on the state of the market comes from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, who publish an annual report about the US market, and that shows this paradoxical situation where the number of policies being issued are growing, but the number or the amount of premium being collected is pretty much stable.

That's really put a lot of companies, a lot of vendors, and enterprises on the defensive. So, what effect is that having?

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I think it's important not to conflate the surge in vulnerabilities being disclosed with a surge in attacks that drive cyber claims, at least not just yet. As many of your listeners will know, not all vulnerabilities are created equal, and so certainly there are thousands more vulnerabilities being disclosed in the months since Mythos preview came out, as compared to earlier in the year, and that's going to have an impact. And you have to look at the high-severity and the critical bugs within that group, and then you have to look at what's actually being exploited as well.

If we want to look at what's a good stand-in for exploitation, you can look at CISA's known exploited vulnerability list. There's a little lag there, but ultimately, if you look at the KEVs, you can see an increase that's happening, but it's not to the same order of magnitude as the overall CVE and vulnerability disclosure. But certainly, there is an increase. I think we just looked at this recently through Sept. 30, and CISA had added 246 KEVs in 2026, which exceeded the 245 added in total for 2025 when we looked at it. So naturally, we are on a trend to exceed last year.

We think maybe it'll be about a third more than last year, when we get to the end of the year, not a trend you want to see, but it's not in the same almost-exponential curve you're seeing with the total vulnerabilities. And I don't mean to be like everything's fine, right?

We also put out a report yesterday, and we look at ransomware leak site data as well as potential indicators of activity, and that's where ransomware threat actors are posting on their Dark Web leak sites who their victims are, and ultimately for Q3 2026, that activity was up. We had 111 distinct groups posting victims. We had a record number of 2,882 victims on leak sites, which is 26% up from the prior quarter and our highest quarter that we've ever seen. So certainly, the activity with the financially motivated threat actors is picking up, and we've also seen that in our business email compromises (BECs) as well, so it's painting a picture of more activity for sure. But just good to note that increased volumes don't necessarily mean increased tax immediately.

DR's Rob Wright: Gotcha. And I'll just say you are allowed to be positive on this podcast. I am going to actually implore you guys to give me some good news as we get deeper into this conversation because I always try to leave these discussions on a positive note, on a high note, rather than doom and gloom. So, we'll see if Daniel brings the doom and gloom now.

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So to bring a bit of gloom, I'd say the conversation also needs to look beyond just vulnerabilities and exploits. AI is a general-purpose technology, and it impacts not just the exploitation of vulnerabilities, but other mechanisms.

So Lauren mentioned an increase in business email compromise, which we've also seen, and we attribute this to in February of this year, a new AI phishing kit was released, EvilTokens, which was basically like a SaaS business model, and they weren't exploiting vulnerabilities. They were using AI to create convincing phishing lures, either by email or often replica websites. They would manipulate the user into letting the attacker in, even if MFA was enforced through either adversary in the middle and phishing, or device code phishing, and then the platform would get access to the mailbox, create mailbox rules, and start to pass through and identify sensitive data.

So this is a way that AI was used at multiple steps. It caused an increase in claims, but it's not actually related to the vulnerabilities that Lauren and you were just talking about. A perfect example. We also attribute that increase in BEC to those tools being made available to threat actors. They are truly too easy to use, unfortunately. EvilTokens was sold as a SaaS business model. So one sophisticated group of criminals built the technology, and they allowed tens, hundreds, thousands of criminals without those skills to use it. And a blockchain tracking company found that they earned $1.1 million in revenue from other criminals buying their services. So, I think this is what Coalition is really worried about when cybercriminals adopt AI into their business models.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: We see that in the ransomware ecosystem, where there's ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS), and so part of what we're looking for is when will the tools become even further identified, and to what extent, who will be doing that? Will it be the ransomware developers? How will that actually get disseminated into the ecosystem? There's a little bit more separation between the original, the victims, and who actually ends up doing the attack at the end, because of the access broker economy and what have you. So, I agree with Daniel. You have to track how these different tools are getting used, and to what extent it has changed the ecosystem.

DR's Rob Wright: So I feel like we're trending in a direction that's less positive. That's OK. But going back to the vulnerabilities, do you feel like customers, like the enterprises out there that are buying insurance, are they aware of what's going on with the threat landscape? Do they know about the surge in reported vulnerabilities, and that the patching windows have decreased? That stuff is getting exploited a lot faster these days. That the risk is generally higher, and that there's a much bigger importance to promptly patching systems. Do they understand that, and do you see them acting on it?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: I would say there's a big range of customers. So, of course, at the high end, you have in the enterprise market customers with a team of threat intelligence specialists who don't really need an insurer to tell them about vulnerabilities being exploited. I think where you really see an awareness gap is small businesses. Many of them don't even have an IT team; they have a website some third-party developer built, and then you see something like the PHP vulnerability in that system, and that's where I think the onus is on the insurer to actively notify those customers that there is a new exposure for them. And that's where, in particular, what Coalition offers is support to actually help them patch those systems, because often for the very smallest customers, they don't have the capabilities to do it.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: That's very well put. I think we're definitely doing our darndest to get the news out to our policyholders at Travelers because that is so important. We similarly have a book that runs the gamut from small businesses and mid-sized businesses, and then large enterprises, and the large enterprises are very aware. With middle market and small companies, I do think the work that we've done and other insurers have done to start that engagement before all of this began will hopefully pay off to some extent.

With our cyber-threat alerts, we're letting them know about any of these new emerging exploits, and then certainly in all of our monthly newsletters and quarterly webinars. This is all we can talk about, is how much faster companies need to be patching, and that their 30-day patch windows or SLAs with their vendors are not going to cut it in this new paradigm. They need to be looking to patch within three days, one day, even for certain types of exploits.

But it is interesting you mentioned PHP, not to have a side here, Daniel. But I find that one so fascinating, because the prevalence on the Web. A full 70% of websites could have PHP as a language within them. What do you do with that? You let everybody know about this vulnerability. You encourage everyone to patch, and I actually totally encourage all the press and the news around it because people were patching more quickly on this vulnerability. But turns out it's been pretty hard to exploit so far, right? And so that's a perfect situation for everyone. Something well-known, pervasive, get it fixed, and fortunately beat that exploitation.

DR's Rob Wright: In addition to shrinking patching windows, faster exploitation, and threat actors using AI to build more effective phishing and BEC attacks … what other risks or major threats do you see your clients facing today, as it pertains to AI?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So, I would start with the rise of open source pen-testing frameworks like Artex. This was developed by a Chinese researcher, and it was actually later taken down because the researcher realized how much it was being abused. But what we've seen is this gives, very unsophisticated actors the ability to draw on more sophisticated pen testing tools that have many agents working in parallel to exploit publicly facing systems. What this pen-testing framework is able to do is test systems, test plug-ins, use a range of tools, and basically throw everything at the system and try every avenue, and the costs are so cheap.

For me, the really worrying thing here is often it's just people playing around. They don't even have the rationale on how to make money from this, and yet from a cyber-insurance perspective, you still have to respond to the claim if they steal data, which often happens. You still have to notify those customers. You'll face a lawsuit. So you have just chaos at the moment with these agentic hacking tools being used to just compromise so many different organizations.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: And it's that experimentation that's happening right now. Once the financially motivated threat actors figure out how they want to harness that type of tool, that's when it becomes more concerning. I think right now we're in the early stages of it. That's translated into not seeing much examples of Artex used for ransomware yet, and they tend to be a little noisier right now, so to the point of the large enterprises who are really on top of things, they're going to identify that very quickly within their systems because it's so noisy.

But these tools are only going to get better, and it's something that looks for the existing vulnerabilities that are already out there, the existing exploits, and that's something that every corporation struggles with already. So again, back to the things we've been preaching for so long: needing to make sure you have good vulnerability management and patch management. That's how you combat these new tools. They're not doing net new ways to attack necessarily. They're using existing methods. They're just agentified and moving fast.

But the other risk, if we're talking about other risks from AI, I look at the inside threat of AI as well. here's a real gap between those that know they're adopting AI and those that have AI governance in place, and I think that's really huge. Whenever you have a technological step-change like AI is, adoption is going to get out ahead of governance, and that creates this risk. There's a lack of visibility for a lot of small businesses and middle-market businesses as to how employees are using these tools. There's a lack of accountability. There's a lack of governance. And we're not yet seeing claims and droves that result from this governance gap. But it's happening, and it's creating this risk, and so you can see how companies are going to start to have employees who put sensitive data into an unsanctioned AI tool.

We know that's happening, and that's going to create a potential data breach, depending on what type of information they're putting into the tool. So that's something that when we're engaging with policyholders right now, we're talking to them about vulnerability management, but we're turning around and trying to assess their actual governance risk as well.

DR's Rob Wright: Daniel, are you seeing similar trends in terms of just not necessarily shadow AI usage, but lack of AI governance?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So, I for sure agree with Lauren. There's a bunch of organizations out there using unsanctioned tools. I think to Lauren's point, there's a bunch of data breaches happening that just will never be reported. They will never end up with a breach attorney who says your notification requirements are X, Y, and Z. I think at the moment, Coalition is more sanguine about that risk just because it's remaining in the shadows for now. I think we're really focused on the business email problem because that's causing the spiking claims at the moment, and also how organizations are going to deal with these open source pen-testing frameworks.

DR's Rob Wright: So a question about agentic AI. I've talked with some companies who are trying to find ways to use AI for good, trying to find vulnerabilities within their products, and develop patches in some cases. I spoke with Ivanti about this recently. Do you guys think that that's a realistic path? Have you, or is that a possibility? Like that we may be able to use some of this technology to remedy vulnerabilities, find vulnerabilities, and fix them before the attackers get them, or is that a long way off?

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I think that's been happening. There are a lot of tech companies that are out ahead of the attackers because they've been running frontier models against their code bases, and then there are also companies that have been running against open source code, right? So there's a plethora of work happening right now to shore up code to ship new patches.

I think one of the problems, though, is for the companies that don't have massive teams who can work on establishing patches. You're told about a new vulnerability. How do you turn around and action that and ship a patch that doesn't have more bugs, right? And so I think that's the spiral we're in right now. There's a bit of a bottleneck, and then companies who are consumers of those tech products then have to do the patches in a lot of cases if it's not a simple cloud update. So, I see this bottleneck happening right now, but it is certainly out ahead of attackers.

That said, some of the models that are out there and in use by attackers now are more sophisticated. So we're at that crux point now, where there are models out there that threat actors can use to identify vulnerabilities and create exploits. And the clock's been ticking, and we're at that intersection.

Coalition's Daniel Woods: Exactly to Lauren's point, there will always be another model that can find new vulnerabilities. Something we're concerned by is, there's been a recent spate of outages. Of course, everyone heard about Microsoft last week. The FAA had an outage, and there's noise that potentially the speed at which organizations are now having to develop and deploy patches is leading to some of these outages. Just because you have to test all of them, and eventually something goes wrong. You test one configuration, then it's pushed to a different server, and that's what causes the outage.

So, although potentially defenders will be able to stay ahead in terms of patching the vulnerabilities, the big concern for cyber insurance is that leads to reliability issues that cause systems failure and business interruptions, which we also cover. So you might solve the security risk, and increase the outage risk.

DR's Rob Wright: I guess the thing I worry about again, and I am a pessimist, so take this with a grain of salt, but is the number of organizations out there that generate the code with AI tools, and push it live without not a lot of human review or really any human review.

And I worry about a future where we're going to have Patch Tuesdays with not just 900 or 1,000 vulnerabilities, but 2,000 or more, and we're just going to be running the code through these AI tools and pushing them out because the sheer number is just too big, and Daniel to your point, not having the quality in place to effectively fix the vulnerability, and also stuff that might screw things up, and you might have outages. That's the panic mode in my brain. Is that something that you guys are worried about, or do you think that we might have the human capability, the human workforce to actually review these patches and the code, and get them in a place that they should be, rather than just pushing them out willy-nilly?

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I think it's important to not talk about it too broadly, right? Tech companies creating tech have an obligation, a responsibility to have software development lifecycles, so it's one thing to be running AI against the code to test it for vulnerabilities and identify them. You need to make sure you have the proper harnesses in place and the proper engineers and humans overseeing that process, and then you want to run it still before it ships to look for vulnerabilities. You need that life cycle. If they're not doing that, that's creating a real problem. But responsible companies who are creating tech responsibly still have their rigorous software development life cycles in place.

Coalition's Daniel Woods: And I think where I would take that is a similar direction. The cyber insurance industry has seen a huge increase in claims related to SSL VPNs provided by a handful of providers who built them in legacy, proprietary operating systems, they never rewrote those that codebase with modern secure software engineering models. And honestly, I think that business model will always be stuck in this reactive cycle. I think what the insurance industry needs to move toward, and it's something Coalition is doing, is shifting organizations toward a more modern approach to developing software, where you build security in early in the process.

So, for instance, a huge amount of vulnerabilities are related to how memory is managed. There are by now completely memory-safe programming languages that vendors can use to build their systems. So, I think the insurance industry needs to move toward rewarding policyholders who are using more modern technology sets. So, we escape the patch cycle because it's just not sustainable to be telling people at 5 p.m. on a Friday you need to patch your systems. Our staff get exhausted from this because they stay up all night notifying people, and then also the people receiving those emails are just as exhausted.

DR's Rob Wright: You mentioned VPNs. I wanted to ask you guys: so obviously, edge devices have been under attack now for a long time, and there have been specific companies and products that have been favorite targets of threat actors. Lots of vulnerabilities, zero-days, etc. Are carriers or the insurance companies approaching a point where you guys might say to a customer, you know what? If you have this in your environment, the risk is too high for us, and just walk away or say that it's a no-go because of certain edge devices or edge products in that environment? Or are we not there yet?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So I would say, for the vast majority, you can build compensating controls in. So we know SSL VPNs are not great. What we would do is work with the customer to update the firmware to the latest version to enforce multifactor authentication or MFA, and then what we would also ask is whether they have running behind that, a modern managed detection and response solution. So if something gets through, you at least detect it and contain it quickly. It's quite rare that we say there's no way we can insure you. It's more about working with the customer, so they're secure enough to offer terms to.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: We take a similar approach as well. We're certainly identifying at the point of underwriting some of the more risky technologies, so that those conversations can be had, those questions can be asked. I'm reaching out to help them understand what a proper patching cadence is going to look like with that edge device that's constantly under attack. What are their plans to move toward something that, in the future, will be more secure? It's not always realistic for a company to move off their VPN quickly, and we recognize that. So it's for those that lean in and say how can I do this securely, and then how can I roadmap to get to where we need to be in the future.

DR's Rob Wright: Last question on AI for you guys. So, we've covered threat actors using AI tools. We've covered the pen testing tools that are available, frameworks, and what it has done to the influx of vulnerabilities. But what about rogue models, agents escaping containment, agents getting into other networks; is that something that you guys have gamed out plans for? Like, if a client is breached by way of an escaped agent, and there's damage or there's data exposed, does it matter who's behind a breach for your customers, or does it become a different calculus when AI is involved?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So, from a coverage perspective, the way cyber insurance policies are worded, the coverage trigger is a security failure, and it's about the victim organization and some unauthorized action being taken on their network.

We never say, we'll cover these kinds of attacks, but not these kinds of attackers. It's always just been about the victim, what did the security incident look like? I don't think this is a coverage conversation.

I think historically the media, and I know we're on a podcast at the moment, has focused on certain kinds of attacks that make great stories, and I think this message that OpenAI was developing a model and it escaped: it makes a great story, but the reality is, for the vast majority of businesses, they're not going to face that kind of threat. I think it's incumbent on cyber insurance to use our data to bring a more sober conversation and focus on how they will actually be compromised: business email compromise, funds transfer fraud, ransomware, and I think that's what we should be helping businesses prevent.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I agree. I think when we talk about the motivations of a rogue agent, it's different than our financially motivated threat actors potentially who are looking to capitalize on that attack. So what that agent does within the environment dictates the response. So, like Daniel said, it doesn't matter if it's a human or an agent. What happened within the environment? What access was had? What data was accessed or exfiltrated or locked up?

I do think, though, there are concerns about agentic use within an organization and when there's agentic drift as well, and that's certainly a known risk, especially among companies that are developing tech. And there are good solutions starting to be built and put into market to help with that monitoring of agents.

But there again, right now in this moment, a lot of companies are lacking that insight and that visibility and that monitoring of agentic behavior, so it's a risk but not something that we're necessarily seeing pronounced in claims yet.

DR's Rob Wright: OK, so let's take a beat and look at 2027. Let's close it out with a look down the road. What do you guys see happening in the next year for the cybersecurity industry, just broadly, Daniel?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: I would expect the increase in frequency of the attacks we've spoken about: business email compromise, phone transfer fraud. The latest evaluations of the very frontier models are finding they can't consistently go from the perimeter of a network to full domain compromise. So I don't think we're going to see automated end-to-end ransomware in 2027. That said, I think there's going to be a lot of chaos, a lot of Web-facing systems breached. They often contain credit-card data, email addresses. So I think it's going to look a lot like the 2010s, more like data breaches, business email compromise.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: If we think about the types of claims that can really drive costs, to what extent are those attacks becoming more and more identified as agentic? Because that necessarily allows threat actors who are financially motivated to have more efficiency and to go after more companies potentially.

Unfortunately, the ransomware threat actors are very successful right now with what they have. And if it ain't broke, don't fix it. So we fully anticipate to see more agentification of different aspects of the attack chain, but that full chaining would be a significant change in this landscape.

DR's Rob Wright: Right. I feel a little bit better about where we are based on what you guys are telling me. Sobering news about how this is going to look more like the 2010s, and we're not going to be having Skynet attacks of rogue agents and models running amok, Daniel. I think you're probably right about that. It's reassuring to hear it. But thank you guys for weighing in on this and giving us a look at what's happening in your industry. Appreciate it.

DR's Becky Bracken: I was going to say, the 2010s don't sound really bad at this point, frankly.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: We had some pretty massive data breaches back then, so I wouldn't seem too eager to go back to that pattern.

DR's Becky Bracken: Oh, something about a BlackBerry though just brought me a sense of comfort. I wanted just to ask, because I am infinitely smarter after this conversation than I was on this topic. So thank you all so much, Rob, for your smart questions and Daniel and Lauren. Your wealth of expertise is invaluable. But I want to ask the question that we started off with, which is: are premiums sustainable? Is the cost of cybersecurity insurance in its current stratosphere, is it sustainable? And what is going to happen with costs in your estimation?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: I don't think the current trend is sustainable, and I think premiums will have to go up. If there are more claims, there are more costs. Insurers need to collect the premiums to cover it.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: And I think that statement was true prior to the frontier AI models. So a lot of insurers within the industry are definitely feeling that that struggle with the current levels of premiums and the current view of risk.

DR's Rob Wright: Although I gotta say, you would think they'd be much higher than they are right now. So I guess that's good. I can't believe I'm being an optimist right now.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: There are other market conditions at play. There are a lot of markets that are selling cyber, and there are new entrants, and that has an impact.

DR's Becky Bracken: Again, you guys have left us all with a lot to think about, from the governance gap to the speed up of patching introducing configuration problems. I think that we're going to be thinking a lot about all of this in the future.

Daniel Woods, head of emerging risk at Coalition; Lauren Winchester, head of cyber risk services at Travelers Insurance; and Rob Wright, senior news director at Dark Reading: thank you all so much for your time and your expertise today, we appreciate it. This has been Dark Reading Confidential, a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I'm Becky Bracken, on behalf of all of us at Dark Reading. Thank you so much for tuning in, and we will see you or hear you next time. Bye.

#9686. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

i discovered this blog two months back from the idscan/Nexus story and was immediately impressed by the journalism on here. as soon as i heard about this doing the rounds elsewhere on social media my first instinct was “i wonder if krebs has written about it yet?” and lo and behold. well anyways, great work as usual, cheers

Maybe I should have kept my blog as pure HTML, perhaps with some perl, instead of going to WordPress.

Just don’t forget the cgi-perl and imagemaps.

Hugo, yes! I finally retired my old Drupal-based site last week and switched to Hugo. For my blog-like site, it’s perfect and saves cost, since it’s served as a static site.

This PHP flaw is a stark reminder of how much of the web runs on shared infrastructure — one critical bug can take government and business sites offline at once. I have been following the patching updates closely, and TrendWire has been a useful source for keeping up with the fast-moving security news around this story. Hopefully hosts patch quickly before mass exploitation ramps up, as the researchers warn.

The vulnerabilities can hardly be referred to as zero-days. They have been known to The PHP Foundation from 2024 but people decided that other bugs were more urgent.

What is fascinating is everyone covering this and sort of ignoring the Indian cert authority issue that made even Krebs hard to POST to days ago. S’okay, timezone and I eligiblegentleman’ed with my cheating billeta hart.

Thanks for the heads-up. I run a small film site on PHP and found out about this from your post, not from my host. If you’re on shared hosting, it’s worth opening a ticket and asking which PHP build they’re actually running instead of trusting the control panel: the version shown there isn’t always the one serving requests.

The scale of this issue makes proactive patch management more important than ever. I’d be interested to see how many affected websites remain unpatched in the weeks following this disclosure.

#9685. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.
