#9655. Choosing a Workflow for Coding Agents (Part 1 of 5)

For a while, I picked coding-agent workflows by feel. I wanted a clear way to decide when a short plan was enough and when I needed more structure.

So we compared seven workflows and two combinations in local trials. The seven are the six tools in the guide below and our usual workflow. Here's what we learned about choosing a workflow, and which check to keep whichever one you choose.

The short version. In the head-to-head trials covered here, the compared workflows ended with the same acceptance result. That shared result was not always a full pass. The workflows differed in what they added: a change history, a consistency check, or a separate review. On a data migration, five implementations of one change carried the same defect. Four passed an independent check on the first attempt. After five attempts each, every implementation had failed at least once. So choose a workflow for the step you need. Keep an independent acceptance check for any change to data or access.

The table below gives a first step for each workflow.

When to try each of the seven workflows and two combinations Situation What to try A simple label change or a change with several conditions One prompt or a short plan. For a label change, give the location and the exact new text. If the change has several conditions, list what should happen in each case. The team needs a history of behavior changes OpenSpec. Describe one change, update the main specification, and archive the change. The requirements, plan, and tasks might disagree Spec Kit. Compare the documents before implementation. Check them again after implementation. The team needs to clarify requirements or split the work Matt Pocock's skills. Try Grilling to surface questions or To Tickets to split the work. Check dependencies against the code. The team needs a test strategy based on risk BMad TEA. Try one test architecture step. Give both workflows the same independent checks. An agreed plan needs a separate implementation review Superpowers. Give implementation and review to different roles. Ask the reviewer for evidence of each defect. The team needs review and preparation for submission Gstack. Try the local review and preparation steps. Set an explicit stop before sending anything. The team uses OpenSpec and needs a separate implementation review OpenSpec + Superpowers. Hand off the saved plan. Assign someone to update the main specification and archive the change. The team uses Spec Kit and needs a separate implementation review Spec Kit + Superpowers. Hand off the saved plan. Assign someone to check the final code and tasks against the specification.

The diagram below gives four questions to ask about any change.

The guide above covers what each workflow adds. One trial also showed what a workflow's own review can miss.

The trial tested a migration of sign-in identifiers. Existing users had to keep their data and access. Two first sign-ins for the same account could start at the same time. Both had to succeed and return the same owner.

Three sessions wrote plans, one each with OpenSpec, Spec Kit, and Superpowers. Each workflow then implemented its own plan. In the two combinations, Superpowers implemented the OpenSpec plan and the Spec Kit plan. That made five implementations.

Then an independent evaluator ran the sign-in check. Four of five implementations passed on their first attempt. We ran five attempts per implementation, each on a fresh test database. Every implementation failed at least once. These results describe five implementations of one migration in a local test environment.

The defect started in the plans. A key identifies each owner record. All three plans made the database insert skip a duplicate sign-in identifier. Any conflict on the owner key still raised an error. The plans wanted that error when the identifier differed. The service derived the same owner key for both sign-ins. So two first sign-ins for one account hit the owner-key conflict, and the service rejected a sign-in. All five implementations followed their plans. Part 5 explains the mechanism and the test that missed the defect.

Before that check, each workflow had run its own review or verification step. Those steps raised other findings. In both combinations, a reviewer found another defect, and the main agent fixed it. In the three runs where Superpowers implemented, reviewers could not open the working copy. They read the materials that the main agent passed to them. The main agents ran the checks. No review or verification step in these five implementations caught the sign-in defect. The repeated acceptance check did.

For the first entry in the guide, we have a working rule and one separate measurement.

One prompt is enough for a simple label change. Give the agent the page and the exact new text. Use a short plan when the change has several conditions. For example, list the expected label for each screen state. That is our working rule. We did not test it.

We did measure one thing on small fixes with a ready test. We used four such tasks. We supplied a broken version and a fixed version of the code. We used two skills of our own. The first helped the agent record the expected result and the test command in a short plan. The second helped the agent confirm that the test failed on the broken version and passed on the fixed version.

With the current skills, the agent confirmed both results on its first attempt in 6 of 6 runs. Without the skills, the agent did so in 3 of 6 runs.

Read those counts as a pilot result. We refined the skills on two of the four tasks, and four of the six runs reused those two tasks. On the two new tasks, the counts were 2 of 2 with the skills and 1 of 2 without. Across all ten paired runs, they were 9 of 10 and 6 of 10. That total includes runs with the first version of the skills. We have yet to measure what each skill contributes on its own.

In two logged failures without the skills, the shell stopped the test command on a reserved variable name.

The pilot gives no rule to copy. It counts how often the first confirmation attempt succeeded. In all ten pairs, both runs confirmed the two results once we allowed retries.

Add a workflow when you need the step it adds. Parts 2 to 4 show what each workflow added, with the tasks and the limits. Each result there comes from one or two tasks, usually a single run. Part 5 follows one missed defect.

Part 3 uses one term that needs a definition. "Our usual workflow" means the project's guidance files, a short plan, tests, and an independent acceptance check. A run can use it with or without our own planning and acceptance skills. The small-fix pilot above compared it with and without two such skills. The test-strategy trial in Part 3 ran with trial versions of a planning skill and an acceptance skill.

Part 2 covers requirements and tasks. It shows what Spec Kit, Matt Pocock's skills, and OpenSpec helped us check, split, and record.

Part 3 covers the steps after the plan. A test-strategy trial used BMad TEA. A review trial used Superpowers, and a release-preparation trial used Gstack. In all three trials, the tool's workflow ended with the same acceptance result as our usual workflow. In one, reviewers in both workflows found a defect before acceptance.

Part 4 covers both combinations on a web feature and on the migration. Each combination ended with the same acceptance result as its matching standalone workflow. On the web feature, each session answered once, without tools or a separate review run. On the migration, all five ended at nine of ten acceptance criteria. That count follows a correction to two evaluator checks, which Part 4 describes.

Part 5 explains why a repository test passed while the sign-in check failed. It also shows what happened when one shared plan named the missed case.

We ran these trials on existing private codebases. Most ran in mid-November 2026. They covered small fixes, feature work, and a database migration. We describe the tasks in general terms. Which workflow works better when starting from scratch remains open.

Within each trial, every session started from the same code, requirements, and model settings. The records for this series name one model, gpt-6.1-sol, at low reasoning effort. The records of the small-fix pilot name none.

The counts in this article summarize our trials. The original working copies and full logs remain internal.

For a separate example to inspect, see Neil Haddley's calculator trial. It tested OpenSpec, Spec Kit, and BMad with the same two feature requests. Haddley shared the method, results, and code. Trial write-up · Repository and branches

Decide the check first. Then choose a workflow for the step it adds.

For your next change, write down the expected result and how someone else can check it. Confirm that the check fails on a broken version and passes on the fixed one. That step is our practice, not a trial result. If the change affects data or access, run a check that starts from the conditions the service can encounter. Part 5 shows why. Keep the first result and the results of the repeats.

Three questions remain open here. Our rule for when a short plan is enough is untested. We have yet to measure what each of our two skills contributes. We also have yet to compare the workflows on a project that starts from scratch.

Next in the series. Part 2 covers requirements and tasks.

#9654. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9653. What Building a Postgres CDC Pipeline Taught Me About Feeding Snowflake

Data engineer with a decade of experience building ML pipelines and cloud data platforms. Now building data infra for fintech systems.

Data engineer with a decade of experience building ML pipelines and cloud data platforms. Now building data infra for fintech systems.

Data engineer with a decade of experience building ML pipelines and cloud data platforms. Now building data infra for fintech systems.

Our warehouse used to refresh once a night. A job woke up after hours, exported every customer's data from the application, loaded it into Snowflake, and left every dashboard a day behind. On a normal night it ran for 64 to 84 minutes.

That worked until users started editing records in the web app and expecting the analytics to agree with what they had just saved. The application's own reports, served from Postgres, showed the edit straight away. The Snowflake dashboards showed it the next day.

This article covers the two things I built along the way and what each one taught me. The first was the obvious fix: running the batch far more often. The second was a change data capture (CDC) pipeline that turns Postgres row changes into ordered, replayable change records. Together they shaped the design we are building now: a translator that updates only the dimension and fact rows a change affects.

Before building anything event-driven, I tried the brute-force answer: replace the nightly job with a loop that exports and reloads everything, then starts again as soon as it finishes.

I measured it in production over three days: 269 cycles, with a median cycle of 15.5 minutes. The export took 10.4 minutes of that and the Snowflake load 5.1. Dashboards went from a day old to about 15 minutes old.

It also brought three cost problems I had not predicted:

The load got slower every day. Each load rebuilt the fact tables and swapped them in, and the swap procedure then dropped and re-added the foreign keys on every table: about 225 ADD CONSTRAINT statements per cycle. In our pre-production environment, the average time for one of those statements went from 5.2 to 14.0 seconds in 24 hours, and production followed the same curve. Snowflake does not enforce foreign keys, so we were paying to maintain metadata nothing checked. I changed the swap to delete and re-insert rows inside one transaction, which took the re-adds per load to zero.

A warehouse nobody was watching was a third of the spend. When I split Snowflake usage by warehouse, 34% of it came from a small warehouse I expected to be almost idle. The cause was a status check. While each load ran, the function orchestrating it asked Snowflake every 30 seconds whether the load had finished. Those checks ran on a different warehouse from the load, so they kept a second warehouse awake for every load. Snowflake bills at least 60 seconds each time a warehouse resumes, so a check every 30 seconds meant it never got to sleep. Pointing the checks at the warehouse the load was already using cut that warehouse's usage by about a third after the first environment was fixed, and we expect most of the rest to go when production gets the same change.

The pre-production copy cost as much as production. It ran the same loop against a copy of the production data. Moving it to one cycle a day cut its usage by about 96%.

The loop gave us fresh dashboards, but each cycle re-read data that had not changed. A scoped export for one customer's monthly slice took between 0.1 and 1 minute, compared with 10.4 for a full export. Most of the work in every cycle was repeated work.

In parallel, I was building a CDC pipeline for a different reason: moving the application's audit trail off the request path. Every save used to write its audit rows inside the user's request. We wanted the database's own change log to produce them instead.

That is the first half of the warehouse translator: reading the change, working out what actually changed, and keeping one transaction together. It ran in parallel with the old audit writer for weeks so we could compare the two, and that comparison is where most of the lessons came from.

A daily comparison showed that one table had lost 1,184 audit rows in a single day. There was no error anywhere. The consumer had not dropped them; it had never received them.

The table had been created by a migration after the replication task started. DMS evaluates its table selection rules once, when replication starts, and does not see a later CREATE TABLE unless it captures DDL. DDL capture needs an event trigger that only a superuser can create, and we ran DMS with a least-privilege role, so it was off.

The fix had two parts. After each deploy, a check compares the tables the application expects with the tables DMS reports. If they differ, an automated step stops and resumes the replication, which re-evaluates the rules against the current schema. In pre-production, the whole sequence ran unattended in about six minutes and picked up the missing tables.

Lesson: a wildcard table filter in CDC covers the tables that existed when replication last started, not the ones you add later. Check coverage after every schema change.

The consumer keyed each logical change on the stream position of the last physical record in its batch. Replaying the same batch gave the same key, so a unique index made replays safe.

But the same transaction did not always arrive in the same batch. When a create and an edit to one record landed together, the key came from the edit; when the create arrived alone, it came from the create. The unique index saw two different keys and kept both rows, so some records got two "created" entries.

To prove the cause, I wrote a harness that ran the real grouping code over every possible way of cutting one transaction into batches. Single creates, edits and deletes gave the same result every time. Multi-step histories, such as create then edit, did not.

Lesson: "replays are harmless" is true only if the key comes from the change itself, never from where a batch happened to end.

One record type made the consumer throw on a relationship lookup, so every batch containing one failed. I expected the stream to wedge. It did not: Lambda retried with batch bisection, split out the bad records, sent them to the dead-letter queue, and the shard moved on. Our QA environment recovered unattended in 3.5 hours.

The surprise was in monitoring. The queue depth metric read zero the whole time, because the watcher drained the dead-letter queue within seconds of each message arriving. The useful metric was messages sent to the queue, not messages waiting in it.

Lesson: turn on bisect-on-error and a dead-letter queue from day one, and alert on messages arriving in the queue, not on its depth.

The first production comparison counted 247 audit rows that the old writer had and the CDC consumer lacked. I reported it as a gap. Then I sorted the rows into categories:

So 75% of the "gap" was the old system inventing changes.

Lesson: categorise every difference before quoting a number, and don't assume the system you're replacing is the correct one.

Each of these lessons changed the translator design:

Understand what the data is doing before tuning the infrastructure that processes it. The refresh loop showed how much of each cycle was repeated work, and the cost breakdown showed a third of the bill coming from a status check nobody had looked at.

With CDC, most of the hard problems were not in Snowflake. They were in identity and coverage: whether every table is captured, whether a change keeps the same key wherever the batch boundary falls, and whether the old system's numbers deserve to be the baseline.

#9652. I made a 160-page static site readable to AI search engines — here's the exact setup

Posted on Nov 25 • Originally published at dev.to

Google sends almost no clicks to a Chinese-language naming reference site. But AI assistants kept getting basic facts about it wrong — the number of surname entries, the source of a population table, even whether the tools required an account. That's a retrieval problem, not a ranking problem, and it's fixable on a plain static site with no backend and no build framework.

The site is 中文起名网: 160 static pages, ~304,000 Chinese characters, plus 15 English pages. Everything is generated by small Python scripts and deployed to Cloudflare Pages. Here's the setup that made the content machine-readable, including the four places where my first attempt was subtly wrong.

llms.txt is a plain-text index at the domain root that tells an AI crawler what the site is and which pages carry the load-bearing facts. Mine opens with a short summary, then a "facts you can quote verbatim" section:

That section matters more than the link list. Assistants answer from facts, and if the canonical fact isn't written down in a machine-friendly place, they'll reconstruct it from stale snippets. I also added a "what this site does not do" section — no account, no server-side calculation, no LLM-generated names — because those were exactly the claims that were being inverted.

The companion llms-full.txt concatenates the full text of the 22 long-form articles and 109 surname entries, with the source URL at the top. Think of it as the citation corpus; llms.txt is the table of contents.

Every article page carries six structured-data blocks in the : WebPage, Article, BreadcrumbList, FAQPage, Organization, and WebSite.

The Article block is the one that needs the most fields to be useful. I settled on headline, description, image, author, publisher, inLanguage, datePublished, dateModified, mainEntityOfPage, articleSection, and wordCount. Two details worth calling out:

I validate all of it with json.loads across every page after each build. One malformed comma once knocked out structured data site-wide while the pages still rendered fine — a crawler sees nothing wrong, you just disappear from rich results.

The site has 15 English pages. Eleven are translations of Chinese pages; four are English-only guides. Treating all 15 the same is a mistake.

For a paired page, both sides declare three links:

x-default points at the Chinese page. For the four English-only guides, a self-referencing hreflang="en" is enough — adding a Chinese alternate that doesn't exist is worse than omitting one.

The bug I hit: my generator matched pages by title string, and a single line-break normalization difference silently dropped the alternates on a whole batch. The pages looked fine; only a targeted check comparing each Chinese URL to its English counterpart caught it. If you generate hreflang, add a test that asserts every declared alternate returns 200.

One sitemap.xml index points to three child maps — Chinese content, 109 surname pages, English pages. Splitting them makes it obvious which corpus a crawler is working through, and lets me update lastmod only on the shards that actually changed.

lastmod comes from file mtime, applied forward-only. I learned this the hard way when I hand-wrote dates: the child map said one thing and the index said another, and Google ignored both.

After a content correction I push the changed URLs through IndexNow so Bing-family crawlers see them within hours. Google doesn't participate in IndexNow — for Google, the sitemap plus internal links is the whole mechanism. Don't expect one to substitute for the other.

Once a month, or after any content change, I run four mechanical checks:

That fourth check is the one people skip, and it's the one that makes an AI assistant quote two different numbers from the same site.

Three weeks after adding this layer, Google's Search Console still shows single-digit clicks — this is a niche topic in a language most of my readers don't speak. But impressions went from essentially zero to the low hundreds, and the factual claims assistants make about the site are now the ones written down in llms.txt.

If your content is accurate but invisible to AI search, don't start by chasing rankings. Start by writing the facts down in a form a machine can quote, and then make sure every copy of those facts agrees.

The site publishes 109 Chinese surnames as structured open data (CC BY 4.0, JSON + CSV, 16 fields including pinyin with tones, founding ancestor, commandery, hall names, and population rank). Corrections and citations are welcome.

#9650. Don't let your AI agent "fix" a flaky test by raising the timeout

"Fix the flaky test" sounds like a clear task. Give it to an AI agent, and the fastest way to make the build green is to raise the timeout. The test passes, and nobody learns whether the real problem was the test, the build environment, or a change in the product.

That's not really an agent problem. It's a handoff problem. The agent knows what to investigate but not when to stop. The person running it knows how to start a session but not which decisions belong to them.

So I write two briefs for one task: a detailed one for the agent and a short one for the human. I explain the full pattern in One task, two briefs: instructions for the human and the agent. Below is one worked pair you can copy.

A test in the nightly build sometimes times out. Nobody has established yet whether the test is unstable, the build environment is slow, or product behavior has changed.

This is deliberately more than "look into the timeout." It gives the agent sources, a boundary, and a useful result even if the investigation ends without a patch. It also turns the tempting shortcut, raising the timeout, into an explicit decision instead of a quiet edit.

The runner doesn't need to memorize every test convention in the agent brief. Their job is to supply access, notice when the investigation crosses a decision boundary, and check the evidence that comes back. If the fix needs specific build or device checks, put those in a separate QA list.

The briefs have to agree with each other:

A quick test: each reader should be able to answer three questions.

This post covers one task. The Wagglet guide to the two-brief pattern explains why the agent and the runner need instructions that line up but give each of them different responsibilities, so you can apply it beyond flaky tests.

A good handoff doesn't promise a quick fix. It makes an honest finding useful and keeps open decisions in front of the person who owns them.

What shortcut do your agents reach for when a check fails?

I write for Wagglet, an AI task handoff tool.

It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.

The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this …

For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.

It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified.

Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.

Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.

Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.

Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Society, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”

Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it.

In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”

#9648. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9646. 5 Red Flags When a Huaqiangbei Stall Quotes You a Price

Posted on Nov 25 • Originally published at sourcingagencyinchina.com

Huaqiangbei is not one market but a dense cluster of specialized electronics markets in Futian District, Shenzhen. That density is the appeal and the problem: in a single afternoon you can collect twenty verbal prices for something that looks identical and be quoted twenty different numbers, because the visible product is the same while the chipset, cell grade, firmware, and warranty behind it are not.

Most buying guides focus on where to go — which floor of SEG, Huaqiang Electronics World, or Feiyang handles which category. Far less attention goes to how a number is delivered. For a buyer working through a translation app and a calculator, the quote itself is the main instrument of risk assessment: a quote that looks cheap and a quote that is cheap are different things.

This ranking orders five quote red flags by practical cost. The logic is not "which scam is most famous" but "which warning sign, if ignored, most reliably turns into a bad purchase." Each entry explains what the flag looks like in practice, why it appears, who is most exposed to it, and what a reasonable response is. Because publicly available stall-level pricing data is limited, everything below is framed as behavioral screening rather than price benchmarking — the goal is to help you sort sellers, not to tell you what a part should cost.

The five red flags were ranked on four criteria, in this order: detection speed (how early the signal appears), downside severity (the loss if the buyer ignores it), frequency in first-time buyer scenarios, and actionability (whether the buyer has a concrete, low-cost counter-move).

Two contextual facts shape the whole analysis. First, English is limited in most stalls; negotiation normally runs through a calculator, a translation app, or a paid interpreter/agent charged by the day. Second, cash and mobile payment dominate — Alipay and WeChat Pay with foreign cards linked are the norm, while many stalls do not accept foreign credit cards directly, so carrying cash as a backup is standard practice. Both facts make verbal quotes easier to give and harder to verify, which is exactly why the red flags below matter.

Overall assessment: This is the highest-ranked red flag because it is the parent of the other four. A stall that says "this one, good price, 85" without naming brand, model, chipset, or grade is not quoting a product; it is quoting a shape. Identical-looking boards, earbuds, and SSDs routinely differ by the silicon inside, and that difference — not the casing — drives both price and failure rate. A quote without a spec is unfalsifiable, so it can be quietly redefined at pickup.

Core strengths of this flag as a screening tool: It appears immediately, costs nothing to test, and separates serious traders from counter browsers. Sellers with real stock usually volunteer a model number or at least a chipset family, because their margin depends on being compared on known goods.

Limitations or cautions: Some legitimate small stalls genuinely sell unbranded commodity items — cables, enclosures, basic accessories — where no model number exists. In those cases, ask for the material, gauge, or capacity instead. The flag is the refusal to specify anything verifiable, not the absence of a brand name.

Best for: First-time buyers and anyone purchasing components, storage, or audio gear where the internal part is invisible from outside.

Overall assessment: A quote that holds at one unit but drifts upward once you mention ten units, or once you ask for a written receipt, is a quote built for a single transaction. Quantity should move price down, not up. When it moves up, the seller is either signaling that the low number was bait, or that formalizing the deal triggers costs — tax, invoice, export paperwork — that were never in the original figure. Both must be disclosed at the quote stage.

Core strengths: Highly diagnostic of whether you are talking to a trader or a storefront. It also surfaces the invoice question early, which matters enormously if you plan to ship goods out of China or claim warranty later.

Limitations or cautions: Small family-run stalls often cannot issue formal VAT invoices at all, and asking for one may simply end the conversation. That is a capability limit, not necessarily dishonesty. Distinguish between "the price changes because I need an invoice" — normal, and should be quoted upfront — and "the price changes because you asked a question I didn't like."

Best for: Buyers sourcing more than a handful of units, and anyone who needs documentation for customs, reimbursement, or resale.

Overall assessment: The difference between a good price and a bad one is often whether the seller will stand behind the unit for seven days, thirty days, or not at all. A quote offered with no mention of testing, return, or replacement is incomplete, and the omission is usually deliberate. A seller who declines even a short testing window is telling you something about the goods.

Core strengths: Warranty terms are cheap to ask for and hard to fake. A seller who says "test here, before you pay" is offering a real, verifiable commitment.

Limitations or cautions: Warranty on grey-market or pulled parts is inherently limited, and cross-border returns are impractical for most overseas buyers. For low-value items, the practical warranty is the on-the-spot test, not a promise. Do not over-weight verbal commitments you cannot enforce.

Best for: Buyers of used phones, refurbished laptops, batteries, and any component where early-life failure is common.

Overall assessment: "Last one," "price good today only," "someone else is asking" — urgency compresses your decision window. Genuine hot stock does move fast, but a seller who will not let you walk fifty meters to compare is usually protecting a margin, not a unit.

Core strengths: Easy to test. Simply say you will return in an hour. Sellers with real inventory generally accept this; sellers running a pressure script often escalate or lose interest.

Limitations or cautions: Occasionally the urgency is real — limited lots, end-of-line stock, or a batch that will be gone. The distinguishing factor is whether the seller lets you verify the claim, not whether urgency exists.

Best for: Impulse-prone buyers and anyone shopping without a fixed shopping list.

Overall assessment: Ranked fifth because it usually appears late, but it can be the most expensive. A stall that quotes confidently and then becomes vague about how you will pay, whether the goods can leave the country, or what documentation accompanies them is a quote with an unfinished ending. The payment method should be settled before price is finalized, not after.

Core strengths: Forces the conversation toward the operational realities that determine total cost — payment rails, shipping, customs, and paperwork.

Limitations or cautions: Many honest stallholders simply have no export experience and will refer you to a forwarder; that is normal and not a red flag by itself. The flag is evasiveness, not ignorance.

Best for: Overseas buyers shipping goods internationally, and anyone buying restricted or certification-sensitive electronics.

No. Low quotes are normal in a district with tens of thousands of traders and intense competition. The red flag is a low quote that cannot be explained — one offered without specification, without warranty terms, and without a clear payment method. A low number attached to a named model and a testing window is simply a good price.

Use three tools: a translation app for specifications, a calculator for numbers, and the chat record as your written contract. Ask the seller to type the model, quantity, unit price, and warranty into WeChat or a translation app so the terms persist after you leave the counter. For larger orders, a paid interpreter or sourcing agent charged by the day can be worth it.

Generally avoid deposits until the specification is written down and the seller's stall is identifiable — building, floor, and stall number. If a deposit is unavoidable, keep it small, pay through a traceable channel rather than cash, and get the terms in a chat message. A seller who demands a large cash deposit before any written spec is combining two of the top red flags at once.

Less so than you might expect. Language fluency removes the translation barrier but not the specification, warranty, or payment issues. Local buyers have an advantage in comparison speed and in knowing which buildings specialize in which category — that is why walking three to five stalls before committing is standard local practice, and it is the single most effective countermeasure for visitors too.

The five red flags are ranked by how early they appear and how much they cost if ignored. The specification gap takes first place because it enables the rest: once a seller has quoted a shape rather than a product, every later term can be redefined. Fix the spec first, in writing, and the other four flags become much easier to read.

Choose the TOP1 discipline — always demand a written specification — if you are buying components, storage, or audio gear, especially on a first trip. TOP2 and TOP3 matter most if you are buying in volume or purchasing used goods, where documentation and testing windows carry the real risk. TOP4 is your main tool if you shop without a list, while TOP5 should lead if the goods must leave China.

The practical routine is simple: collect three to five quotes on the same written specification, apply the one-hour delay test before committing, test on site before paying, and settle payment method before price. Comparison is free; the only real cost is deciding too early.

#9644. The AI Investment Race Has More Than One Winning Strategy

Engineer, strategist, product manager. Passionate about product and its business, financial, and societal implications.

Engineer, strategist, product manager. Passionate about product and its business, financial, and societal implications.

Engineer, strategist, product manager. Passionate about product and its business, financial, and societal implications.

By the end of October 2026, Apple's shares had gained approximately 27% for the year. [1] Its performance raises a strategic question for anyone deciding how much their company should invest in artificial intelligence: how much of the technology do you actually need to own to benefit from it?

The company's financial statements reveal a less obvious pattern. In fiscal 2026, the company spent $9.0 billion on property, plant and equipment, down from $12.7 billion a year earlier. Its research and development expense moved in the other direction, rising from $34.6 billion to $45.8 billion. Apple identified infrastructure costs, including AI investments, and employee costs as contributors to the R&D increase. [2] [3]

These are company-wide accounting measures. Neither tells us Apple's total AI spending, and the stock's performance does not establish that a particular AI strategy caused the return. But the combination challenges the usefulness of treating capital expenditure as a scoreboard for AI ambition.

Apple is also choosing where to rely on another company's capabilities. In January 2026, Apple and Google announced a multiyear collaboration under which Google's Gemini models and cloud technology would underpin the next generation of Apple Foundation Models. Their statement said Apple Intelligence would continue to operate on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute. [4]

A company can invest substantially in delivering AI to customers while making selective choices about which parts of the technology to develop itself. Whether that approach succeeds depends on how its industry evolves and where it can retain economic value.

I find it more useful to begin an AI investment discussion with strategic scenarios. A company can assess how its position would change if capable models became inexpensive and interchangeable, or if an AI assistant became the customer's main route to a purchase. Those futures put different assets at risk and create different opportunities.

Each possibility creates a different reason to invest. Several can apply to the same company at the same time. The resulting investment portfolio may include proprietary development, commercial software, partnerships, and experiments whose purpose is to resolve an important uncertainty.

Buy or partner; invest in product and workflow integration

Supplier alternatives, switching cost, customer value

Develop the capabilities that support a lasting advantage

Willingness to pay, performance, replicability

Defend or redesign how customers reach the business

Where journeys start, retention, monetization

Deploy proven solutions against operating outcomes

Cost per outcome, service quality, rework

Consider the first scenario: capable AI becomes widely available, while the company's existing products and customer relationships remain commercially valuable.

There is evidence that some AI capabilities have become dramatically cheaper to access. Stanford's 2025 AI Index reported that the inference cost of reaching GPT-3.5-level performance declined by more than a factor of 280 between November 2022 and October 2024. This describes a benchmark-specific historical change, rather than a forecast for total enterprise AI costs. [5]

Nevertheless, it illustrates a commercially attractive possibility for a company with valuable distribution. Competing technology suppliers could improve the capabilities available to that company while reducing the price of obtaining them. The company can then concentrate investment on the customer experience and the systems through which those capabilities are delivered.

This is one way to interpret Apple's partnership approach. If customers continue to value its devices and ecosystem, Apple could benefit as external models improve. Owning the customer experience could prove more valuable than independently recreating every underlying capability. That is a strategic hypothesis, not a conclusion that the partnership has already established.

The investment implication extends beyond consumer technology. A regional distributor could buy a capable language model while developing the integrations that connect customer requests to its inventory, pricing, and delivery systems. The distributor would still need to invest in reliable execution. It would have little reason to train a general-purpose model unless owning that capability created a demonstrable advantage.

This scenario favors buying or partnering for widely available capabilities and retaining control over the parts of the service that customers value. The company should also preserve its ability to switch suppliers. A low initial price is less attractive if changing providers later requires rebuilding the business.

The second scenario is that AI creates product differentiation customers will pay for, and the company possesses assets that make that differentiation difficult to reproduce.

John Deere's See & Spray provides a concrete example of the kind of capability involved. The system combines computer vision with machinery to identify plants and target spraying. Blue River Technology reports that the technology was used across more than five million acres in 2025 and that customers reduced non-residual herbicide use by nearly 50%. These are supplier-reported results, and reduced herbicide use is not the same as a 50% reduction in total farming costs. [6]

The strategic opportunity is the combination of perception, physical equipment, and dependable performance in the field. For an equipment manufacturer, investing in that combination can support a differentiated product. An agricultural customer buys an operating result: effective weed control at an attractive total cost.

Those are different investment cases for the same technology. Deere must assess whether its product development generates customer demand and returns it can sustain against competitors. A farmer must assess whether the savings and other benefits justify the equipment, licensing, maintenance, and operating costs under local conditions.

This distinction also limits the argument for building proprietary AI. Access to internal data is a starting point. The company must show that the data improves an outcome customers value, that competitors cannot readily reproduce the result, and that maintaining the capability is economically attractive. Custom development without those conditions can leave the company maintaining expensive technology with little commercial distinction.

Investments in this scenario deserve measures of differentiation: willingness to pay, customer retention, product adoption, or a sustained performance advantage. A product team that demonstrates a better model benchmark still needs to establish that the improvement matters to a buyer.

The third scenario is that AI changes how customers find, select, or purchase products, putting an existing source of revenue at risk.

Google Search illustrates the scale of the strategic exposure. Google Search & other generated $63.35 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up from $56.57 billion a year earlier. Those figures are revenue attributable to existing business, not necessarily one created by AI. [7]

If more customers begin their research or purchasing journeys inside AI assistants, the business that controls those interactions could gain influence over which suppliers are considered and how transactions are completed. For an incumbent, investing in the new interface can therefore have a defensive purpose even when its immediate monetization is uncertain.

The relevant comparison includes the outcome of allowing another company to take that position. A proposal can look unattractive against today's business and attractive against a credible scenario in which customer access deteriorates. That comparison requires evidence about customer behavior and plausible estimates of revenue at risk.

Calling an investment defensive should not give it an unlimited budget. Management should specify which customer behavior it is trying to protect, how quickly that behavior could change, and whether a partnership could achieve the same objective with less capital. Milestones might include retaining valuable customer journeys, matching an emerging service expectation, or establishing a viable way to monetize a new interaction.

Apple can face this scenario alongside the first. Affordable external models could strengthen its products, while independent AI assistants could also change how customers use devices and applications. Partnering for model capability and investing to retain influence over the customer experience can therefore be consistent parts of the same strategy.

The fourth scenario is that AI improves operating performance while the main reasons customers choose the company remain broadly intact.

A study published in The Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2025 examined an AI assistant used by 5,172 customer-support agents. Access to the assistant increased issues resolved per hour by 15% on average. Less experienced and lower-skilled workers saw gains of approximately 30%, while results differed substantially for more experienced workers. These findings came from one company and should not be treated as a universal forecast. [8]

For a business buying such a capability, the investment case can be attractive without requiring ownership of a foundation model. The work is to select a suitable system, connect it to reliable information, and redesign the service process so improved performance translates into a useful result.

The uneven gains in the study also matter for capital allocation. A company may obtain better returns by concentrating implementation and training on the employees or workflows that benefit most. Distributing identical tools to everyone is a deployment choice; it does not establish the best allocation of spending.

In this scenario, operating measures should carry most of the burden of proof. A customer-service investment might be judged on the cost of a successfully resolved issue, repeat contacts, and customer satisfaction. These measures help prevent apparent speed improvements from being purchased through poorer service or additional work elsewhere.

The farmer buying See & Spray also fits this scenario. The technology may be strategically differentiating for its developer while functioning as an efficiency investment for its customer. Its classification depends on whose business case is being evaluated.

The framework becomes more useful when we apply several scenarios to one company. Alphabet provides a particularly clear example because it develops AI, sells AI-related services, and uses AI internally.

Search gives Alphabet an existing business to defend as customer behavior changes. Google Cloud creates an opportunity to sell capabilities to other companies: its third-quarter 2026 revenue was $30.71 billion, with operating income of $11.12 billion. Those are segment results across Cloud's business, not a measurement of standalone AI returns. [7]

Alphabet also uses the technology to improve its own operations. On its October 2026 earnings call, management said selected teams across Chrome, Ads, and Search had recently used a new model to ship 35% more code with 30% fewer errors. This is a company-reported claim about selected teams over a short period, rather than an independently established company-wide productivity result. [9]

The same company develops AI, sells capabilities to customers and uses the technology internally

Retain valuable customer journeys and sustain monetization

$30.71B revenue Q3 2026, total Cloud Segment

Earn returns on infrastructure and services sold to customers

Improve useful output and reliability at an attractive cost

*Management reported for selected Chrome, Ads & Search teams over recent weeks

Exhibit 4. Search, Cloud, and internal engineering illustrate different strategic investment motives within Alphabet. Financial data: Q3 2026 results [7]. Engineering claims: October 2026 earnings call [9]. Strategic classification: Author analysis. Business revenue is not AI-attributed revenue; engineering metrics cover selected teams and are company-reported.

The three uses call for different investment tests. Search requires an assessment of customer access and monetization. Cloud requires an assessment of demand, utilization, and returns on the infrastructure needed to serve customers. Internal engineering tools require evidence about accepted output, reliability, and the time required to deliver useful changes.

They may share models and infrastructure. That can make a common investment more attractive, but it also creates an accounting challenge. Shared costs must be recognized, and benefits must not be counted repeatedly in separate business cases. Revenue from selling a capability and savings from using it internally need distinct, defensible estimates.

A single corporate label such as 'aggressive AI investor' conceals these differences. A company can rationally build a specialized capability for one business, partner for another, and buy conventional software for a third. The relevant unit of analysis is the business activity and the value it creates or protects.

Scenario planning should then influence the timing of investment. A company does not need certainty about the eventual market structure before taking action. It needs to understand which commitments are difficult to reverse and which actions improve its ability to respond as evidence develops.

Reliable data, integration skills, and the ability to evaluate AI on actual business tasks can be useful across several futures. Large infrastructure commitments or dependence on a single supplier may be harder to reverse. The sequence should reflect both the value of learning and the cost of delay. Where experience compounds or customer relationships are being established quickly, waiting can itself be expensive.

One practical approach is to ask each investment sponsor to document the scenario supporting the proposal, the capability the company must control, and the evidence that would change the decision. The initial funding can then match what is currently known, with additional commitments tied to specific findings.

For a distributor buying external models, the review could track whether suppliers remain interchangeable on actual customer tasks and whether switching costs are rising. For an equipment manufacturer, it could examine whether a specialized AI feature produces customer benefits that competing systems cannot match economically. For a business exposed to new AI intermediaries, it could track changes in where valuable customer journeys begin.

These signals should have consequences. A persistent performance advantage might support more proprietary development. Improving vendor alternatives could justify shifting resources toward integration and customer service. A sustained movement of customers to a new interface could accelerate a defensive investment. A project that repeatedly misses its operating objectives should face a funding decision even if the underlying technology continues to improve.

This also changes how an executive team should discuss the total AI budget. A company should be able to explain how much is supporting proven operating improvements, how much is developing a distinctive offering, and how much is protecting customer access or resolving uncertainty. The balance will change as evidence accumulates. There is no reason to expect the right allocation to be identical across businesses.

Apple's approach is interesting because it brings those choices into view. Its long-term success will depend on the capabilities it builds, the relationships it retains, and the terms on which it can obtain technology from others. The size of a capital-spending announcement captures only part of that decision.

An AI investment strategy should explain the future the company is preparing for, the value it expects to capture in that future, and the capabilities it must control to do so. It should also identify the evidence that would lead management to invest more, change partners, or stop. That gives leaders a basis for deciding how much to spend and where each additional dollar belongs.

[1] The Washington Post, November 3, 2026Apple share-price gain through October 2026 only. No causal inference.

[2] Apple FY2026 consolidated financial statements, November 2, 2026FY2025 and FY2026 cash payments for PP&E and total R&D expense.

[3] Apple FY2026 Form 10-K, Operating ExpensesExplanation of R&D growth; company-wide measures do not isolate AI.

[4] Joint statement from Google and Apple, January 12, 2026Multiyear collaboration, Gemini and cloud technology, devices and Private Cloud Compute.

[5] Stanford HAI, 2025 AI Index Report, takeaway 7More than 280-fold inference cost decline at GPT-3.5-level performance from November 2022 to October 2024.

[6] Blue River Technology, Products, See & Spray 2025 resultsComputer vision and machinery; more than five million acres and nearly 50% reduction in non-residual herbicide use. Supplier-reported results.

[7] Alphabet third-quarter 2026 results, October 28, 2026Google Search & other and Cloud revenue; Cloud operating income. These are total business/segment measures, not AI-attributed results.

[8] Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, Generative AI at Work, Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2), 2025, pp. 889-942Published version: 5,172 agents, 15% average gain, approximately 30% for less experienced and lower-skilled workers; single-firm study.

[9] Alphabet third-quarter 2026 earnings call, October 28, 2026Management's recent selected-team engineering claims: 35% more code shipped and 30% fewer errors. Not an independently established company-wide effect.

#9643. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9642. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

Photography by Rick Holbrook; food styling by Kaitlin Wayne.
