#9641. Keeping Requirements and Tasks in Sync with Coding Agents (Part 2 of 5)

A web app fails to load data. The user retries, and the data arrives. Should the app resume work the user already requested? What should happen to an unsubmitted form?

We faced that decision in a local trial. We agreed to keep the input and resume work only after the user had submitted the form. A draft plan still missed recovery cases. A task list that one tool proposed made two screens wait for a third. Both could start once two shared pieces were ready.

The short version. Pick the tool by the job.

We observed these steps in two local trials on existing codebases. The first two sections use a web recovery trial. The next two use a separate command-line trial. Both used gpt-6.1-sol at low reasoning effort.

Four step names appear in the first two sections. Clarify and Analyze are Spec Kit steps. Clarify asks questions about a specification and records the answers. Analyze compares the specification, plan, and tasks, and reports where they disagree. Grilling and To Tickets are two of Matt Pocock's skills. Grilling asks questions in rounds. To Tickets drafts tasks with their dependencies and acceptance checks. OpenSpec, in a later section, keeps a main specification and a separate folder for each change.

In the web recovery trial, we did not install Spec Kit in the project. Each session received the instruction file for one step, at a fixed version. So that trial shows what the instructions and our prompt produced. It does not confirm how an installed Spec Kit or installed skills behave. In the command-line trial, OpenSpec and Spec Kit were set up in their working copies.

We ran Spec Kit's Analyze step on the agreed web recovery specification, a draft plan, and a draft task list. We had written those short drafts before we agreed the answers, and we left them unchanged. So the drafts were out of date. Our prompt told Analyze that they were unchanged. Analyze found that the plan missed some updated requirements. The plan also left the behavior after a second failed load unclear.

The feature covered three screens: a form, a saved list, and a search screen. Here is one draft requirement and the search part of the text we agreed. We reworded it slightly. None of the four steps wrote the agreed text. The next section describes the question rounds that used those answers.

Example: a requirement in the draft and after agreement

Analyze reported that no task covered the search screen or a recovery check with the same filters. The agreed requirement gives the reviewer an outcome to verify.

Try this when the specification and task list may describe different behavior. Pick one requirement. Find the task that implements it and the test that checks it.

In the web recovery trial, we gave Grilling and Spec Kit's Clarify the same starting material. We answered from a shared set of agreed responses. Grilling raised questions about keyboard focus and actions on another screen. We stopped it after two rounds, with three questions still open. Clarify returned draft requirements with concrete checks. The environment prevented it from writing the specification directly. Our final message to each tool carried acceptance checks from the same agreed set.

Once the requirements were agreed, To Tickets turned the retry and recovery rules into acceptance criteria for three tasks. Its task list made work on two screens wait for a third screen. The code showed that both screens needed the same data loader and retry control. Both could proceed once those shared pieces were ready. We checked the dependency against the finished implementation of the feature.

Try Grilling when you still have a decision to make. Save the answers and mark the questions that remain open. Try To Tickets when the behavior is clear enough to divide. Ask what concrete result each dependent task needs. Then check that dependency in the code.

This was one web feature. We ran Analyze and To Tickets once each on the agreed requirements, and we knew which tool produced each result. Grilling ended early, and the task drafts never went to an issue tracker during the trial. We observed improvements to the drafts. We have yet to measure whether they lead to less rework during implementation. Matt Pocock's skills repository

The command-line trial added a new reporting command to an existing repository. The command read logs of agent runs.

Converge is the Spec Kit step that checks the code against the specification, plan, and tasks, then adds missing tasks. In this trial, Converge found that an open task had left the local package unfinished. It added a follow-up task. The task covered running the documented command and proving that the input files stayed unchanged. A second Converge run left the task list unchanged.

Before you close the work, trace one requirement to its task and test again. Analyze and Converge showed two kinds of gaps. Two examples cannot show how often Spec Kit catches similar gaps across projects. Spec Kit's workflow and supported scenarios

OpenSpec ran in the same command-line trial, in its own session. The task contract said what the report should do when a file was missing.

One rule mattered. Two entries could refer to the same run even if one file was missing. The report had to count that run's confirmed usage once. It also had to report that its data was incomplete. The order of the entries could not change that result.

The OpenSpec agent checked the change and created the main specification. That file now states the rule, with a scenario for both orders of the entries. The agent then moved the completed change into the archive. The archived folder keeps the proposal, the design, and the tasks behind the rule.

The agent archived the change by moving files, as the archive skill instructs. The log shows no call to OpenSpec's archive command. So this run shows the skill at work, not the command.

How we tested the archive command We restored the state after the specification update in a separate copy and tested the archive command there. The command ran with its specification update switched off and created the archive.

We restored the state after the specification update in a separate copy and tested the archive command there. The command ran with its specification update switched off and created the archive.

If you try this workflow, give the next session two questions. Where does it find the current rule? Where does it find the change that introduced the rule? We checked the files when the work ended. The trial did not follow a new maintainer through later changes. This trial was one case, with one run per approach. OpenSpec quickstart

For the web recovery feature, the next session should be able to find three things. We took them from our trial records. We did not ask a fresh session to find them.

Try the handoff check with one requirement when a piece of work ends. Ask a fresh session to name the decision, the dependency, and the check from the saved files alone. That check is our suggestion, not a trial result.

The next comparison should follow one feature through several changes and a handoff. That would show which decisions the next session can recover and which the team has to explain again.

Next in the series. Part 3 covers the steps after the plan: test strategy, review, and release preparation.

#9640. How to Test Signup and Checkout Forms With Fake Addresses (Without Using Your Real One)

Every developer has been there. You're building a signup form or a checkout flow, and you need to test it. The form asks for a full address — street, city, state, ZIP code, country. You could type your own real address, but you don't want your personal data sitting in a test database, a staging log, or a screenshot shared in a pull request. You could type random gibberish, but then your validation logic never gets exercised properly, and your layout never sees realistic data.

The practical answer is fake address data: addresses that look and behave like real ones but belong to nobody.

A form that accepts "asdf 123" tells you almost nothing. Real addresses have structure — a street number and name, a city that actually exists in the chosen state, a ZIP code with the right format for that country, and a phone number with a plausible area code. When you test with data shaped like the real thing, you catch the bugs that matter:

Here's a simple workflow that works whether you're testing by hand or writing automated tests:

1. Generate a complete fake address. Use a free fake address generator to get a full, consistent profile in one click — street address, city, state, ZIP code, and country that all fit together. One click gives you a fresh set, so every test run can use different data.

2. Fill the form exactly as a user would. Paste the generated values into each field. Don't skip the optional ones — apartment numbers and second address lines are where layout bugs hide.

3. Test the unhappy paths too. Try a ZIP code from a different state than the city. Leave the street empty. Enter a very long street name. A good generator gives you fresh data each time, so you can repeat these cases quickly without inventing new addresses by hand.

4. Test internationally. If your form supports multiple countries, generate addresses for different countries and check that your field labels, formats, and validation rules adapt — a UK postcode looks nothing like a US ZIP code.

5. Keep test data out of production. Fake addresses are fictional by design, so there's no risk if they linger in a staging database. Still, keep a habit of clearing test data regularly — clean staging data makes debugging easier for everyone.

The rule is simple: never use real people's addresses for testing, even your own, unless you have to. Test databases get copied, exported, screenshotted, and shared far more often than anyone plans. Fictional data generated for testing carries none of that risk, and it costs nothing — the tools are free, need no sign-up, and run entirely in your browser.

One important limit: fake phone numbers that come with generated profiles cannot receive calls or SMS. That's by design. If your flow needs a one-time code, use your own number for that one step, or use a dedicated test number from your SMS provider's test range. Everything else — the name, the address, the form filling — can be fake.

An address rarely travels alone in a form. Signup and checkout flows usually ask for a name, an email, and sometimes a phone number as well. Generating a matching set keeps your tests consistent — the same fictional person across every field. A random name generator covers the name field, and the same site offers a fake phone number generator for the phone field, so you can build a complete test profile in seconds instead of inventing one field at a time.

Designers benefit from the same trick. Mockups, prototypes, and demo screenshots look far more convincing with a realistic address than with "John Doe, 123 Test St." Clients and stakeholders react to realistic data because it looks like the finished product.

Pick one form in your project — a signup, a checkout, or a profile settings page. Generate three different fake addresses and submit the form with each. Check what lands in your database, what shows in your logs, and how the confirmation screen renders the address. If all three pass cleanly and nothing real leaked into the data, your form handling is in good shape. If something breaks, you've found a bug before a real user did — and it only cost you five minutes.

FakeXLab offers free fake data generators — including a fake address generator, a password generator, and a UUID generator — that run entirely in your browser with no sign-up required. All generated data is fictional and intended for testing and design purposes only.

#9639. opencode-plugin-memory 0.7.0: memory that follows you across repos

Posted on Nov 25 • Originally published at jczhu.com

opencode-plugin-memory gives an OpenCode agent memory that a human has to approve: the agent proposes an entry, a bot opens a pull request, you merge it. Markdown in Git, no vector database.

0.7.0 is the biggest release since the first version. Until now that memory lived inside one repository. Now it can live in two places at once.

A proposal names its store and picks global by default once the clone exists. Everything else keeps working: with no global clone, memory stays inside each project exactly as it did in 0.6.0, and the prompt says so in one line instead of failing.

The split matters because knowledge has two lifetimes. How an API behaves, or a review rule you hold everywhere, belongs in global. A repository's architecture and business definitions belong to it alone.

Both indexes now share one character budget. The global section is capped at a configurable share (70% by default), and the project section keeps at least the rest reserved, so a large global store can never push project entries out of the prompt. Budget one side does not need flows to the other, and a truncated section says so instead of silently vanishing.

Publishing now covers every store with pending proposals and returns the pull request links grouped by store. A global proposal opens its pull request in your private memory repository; a project proposal opens it in the project repository.

Each store has its own staging folder, lock, and publish state, so a failure in one never blocks the other.

Memory is for what the code cannot say. If a rule will be stated by the code, the tests, or a design document once it is built, it does not belong in memory, because a second copy drifts at the next refactor.

0.7.0 makes that a first-class retirement reason. implemented means the artifact took over: the pull request is marked as graduated, so a reviewer sees the memory is leaving because the code replaced it, not because the rule stopped being true.

The bot works in a throwaway git worktree and only removes worktrees it can prove it created. If Git refuses a removal, it leaves the directory alone. A leftover worktree from an earlier crash no longer blocks later runs, and an unreadable memory file is counted and skipped instead of taking the whole index with it.

No action is needed. Existing project memories stay where they are.

If you want the global store, create a private repository, clone it to ~/.local/share/opencode/memory, and give it memory/active/, memory/retired/, and a .gitignore containing .memory/. The next session picks it up without a restart. Prefer the old behavior? Turn the global store off.

These are the words still up for grabs. Neither meaning has more than 60% of the combined Wikipedia attention, and they're ranked by how close each fight is to a perfect 50/50. #9637. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

Find puerquitos and many more Mexican sweets in our feature celebrating pan dulce.

#9636. How End-to-End Encryption Works in an Android Chat App (ECDH + AES-GCM in Kotlin)

Short answer: end-to-end encryption (E2EE) means only the two people chatting can read the messages, not even your server. Each device creates a key pair, they exchange public keys, each side computes the same shared secret with ECDH, derives an encryption key from it, and encrypts every message with an authenticated cipher such as AES-GCM. The server only ever sees ciphertext.

This article explains each step in plain language and shows the Kotlin code using only standard Android APIs.

I'm Padmakar Garg, a Senior Android Developer. I work on secure messaging, encrypted calling and Android security. The code below is for understanding how E2EE works. For production, use a vetted protocol and library (see the end).

The magic is that Alice and Bob end up with the same secret without ever sending it. The server relays public keys and ciphertext, and cannot compute the secret.

Each device creates an elliptic-curve key pair. The private key never leaves the device.

To send the public key to the other user, encode it to bytes. To receive one, decode it:

Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) combines your private key with their public key. The maths guarantees both sides get the same result.

Alice calls sharedSecret(A_priv, B_pub) and Bob calls sharedSecret(B_priv, A_pub). The two byte arrays are identical.

Never use the raw ECDH output as an AES key. Run it through a key derivation function (KDF) such as HKDF. Here is a small HMAC-SHA256 based version for a 32-byte key:

The info string binds the key to its purpose, so the same secret can never be reused accidentally for something else.

AES-GCM gives you confidentiality and integrity in one operation. If anyone modifies the ciphertext, decryption fails.

Use the chat ID and message ID as the aad (additional authenticated data). That way a ciphertext cannot be moved to another conversation without detection.

In GCM, one repeated IV with the same key can leak plaintext relationships and break authentication. Use a fresh random 12-byte IV for each message, or a strict counter, and rotate keys regularly.

If the server hands you the wrong public key, it can sit in the middle and read everything (a man-in-the-middle attack). Let users compare a fingerprint (for example a hash of both public keys) out of band:

Show it as a "safety number" that two people can compare in person or on a call.

If one long-term key leaks, an attacker could decrypt all past messages. Use ephemeral keys per session and rotate them as messages flow. The Signal protocol does this with the Double Ratchet algorithm.

Never keep private keys in SharedPreferences or a plain file. Use the Android Keystore where supported. ECDH operations inside the Keystore need a recent Android version, so check the documentation for the API level you support.

E2EE protects message content. The server can still see who talks to whom, when and how often, unless you design for that separately.

Writing your own protocol is risky, because tiny mistakes are invisible and fatal. For a real app, prefer:

Use the code in this article to understand what those libraries do, not to replace them. If you want to see a protocol implemented from a specification, I've published a Kotlin SDK implementing the MTProto 2.0 primitives (AES-IGE and Diffie-Hellman key exchange) here: github.com/gargpadmakar/MTProtoCrypto.

#9632. Your Lead Score May Be Learning Who Sales Already Chose to Call

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Hero illustration. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

Consider a hypothetical company that trains a lead score on historical customers. The model discovers that contacts from a favored segment are more likely to progress. Sales receives more contacts from that segment, calls them sooner, and creates more opportunities there.

The next training cycle sees the same pattern more strongly.

That pattern could reflect real demand. It could also reflect where the company invested its attention. Historical success does not explain the difference by itself.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

I would not reject lead scoring because of this problem. I would ask a more precise question before allowing a score to allocate scarce sales capacity: what process produced the labels that the system is learning to predict?

Consider the label sales-qualified lead. It may represent a carefully verified need. In another organization, it may represent a rep clicking a lifecycle field after a first call. A label with the same name can encode different decisions.

Even a clear commercial outcome sits downstream of company actions. Routing, response time, territory coverage, pricing, product availability, and follow-up quality can affect who reaches that outcome. A model trained on the history may learn useful correlations without separating those mechanisms.

HubSpot's AI score documentation describes generating criteria and points from account contact data using a selected lifecycle transition. That makes the chosen transition an important modeling decision, not an administrative detail.

The implication is my analytical interpretation, not a claim that HubSpot's model has a particular defect: if the business meaning of the transition is unstable, the score's target is unstable too. Review the process behind the field before debating whether the suggested points look sensible.

Imagine a fictional business with two lead groups. Both contain potential buyers. Group A receives a fast response and several useful conversations. Group B is routed to an understaffed queue, where many records receive no meaningful follow-up.

If Group A progresses more often, that observation alone does not establish how Group B would perform under the same treatment. Nor does it establish that moving every Group B record into the fast queue would produce the same result.

Start by auditing the exposure to company action: assigned owner, attempted contact, reached contact, response delay, and relevant follow-up where those facts are available and appropriate to use. Missing activity is not always proof that no activity occurred, so mark coverage limitations.

Distinguish a negative outcome from an unresolved one. A prospect who declined after a relevant conversation is not equivalent to a lead that nobody reached. A lead created yesterday should not be labeled a failure merely because its outcome window has not elapsed.

This review does not solve causal inference. It tells the team whether its training labels mix meaningfully different situations and where stronger evaluation may be needed.

The sales-attention feedback loop. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

The most flattering model can be the one that has accidentally seen the future. A property added during a sales conversation may predict the later opportunity extremely well, but it cannot help prioritize the call that produced the property.

The scikit-learn guide to data leakage explains the general problem: information unavailable at prediction time can create overly optimistic evaluation. The principle applies whether a team uses that library, a managed product, or a spreadsheet.

Define a scoring timestamp and reconstruct the feature values available then. Keep event time separate from ingestion time. A warehouse record loaded on Friday may describe an interaction that occurred on Tuesday, while a value overwritten on Thursday may hide what was visible on Wednesday.

For a custom evaluation, inspect high-performing features for timing. Deal creation, later lifecycle stages, post-call qualification fields, and completed onboarding steps may belong to the outcome process rather than the pre-call decision.

Do not assume every predictive feature is leakage. A confirmed budget recorded before the scoring time can be legitimate. The test is availability and permitted use at the actual decision point, not whether the feature seems unusually informative.

HubSpot's scoring overview distinguishes engagement, fit, and combined scores, with capabilities depending on subscription and record type. These scores can be useful for prioritization without representing a calibrated chance of winning.

A score of eighty should not be presented as an eighty-percent probability unless the system and evaluation support that interpretation. Ranking quality and probability calibration answer different questions.

The scikit-learn calibration documentation provides the statistical distinction. A model can rank cases usefully while its stated probabilities fail to match observed frequencies. Calibration itself requires appropriate held-out evaluation.

For a marketing team, the practical consequence is simple. Name the output according to what it is. Priority score is safer than probability of purchase when the number is a weighted set of criteria. An AI-generated explanation should not upgrade the score's meaning in its prose.

This also affects thresholds. A cutoff chosen because sales can review fifty records is a capacity decision. It should not be described as a natural boundary between buyers and nonbuyers.

A global accuracy number can hide a poor allocation decision. If sales works only a small top-ranked queue, inspect the quality and coverage of that queue. If the score triggers nurturing rather than a call, evaluate the relevance and consequences of that different action.

Keep a later evaluation period separate from training and tuning. For custom models, ensure preprocessing and feature selection respect the split. When records from the same company are strongly related, consider whether a random contact split allows account-level information to leak across the boundary.

Report uncertainty and sample sizes. Three wins in a tiny group do not establish that a model works equally well there. An absence of observed failures can reflect a lack of evaluated cases.

The evaluation should also account for lead maturity. Compare cohorts with sufficient time to reach the defined outcome rather than rewarding the oldest records for having had more opportunities to progress.

Before changing routing, calculate the proposed score alongside the current process without allowing it to drive consequential actions. Record what it would recommend and why. This is shadow evaluation, not a controlled estimate of incremental value.

Review disagreements. Which promising-looking leads rank low? Which high-ranked leads have only noisy email activity? Are important product segments missing from the training history? Does the explanation depend on a property that sales fills only after qualification?

Then decide whether a limited, appropriately designed comparison is justified. A randomized routing experiment may be useful in some settings, but it requires ethical treatment, operational capacity, adequate measurement, and a clear fallback. Do not casually withhold responses to explicit requests for help.

If experimentation is not feasible, document the narrower evidence available. An observational comparison can guide improvement without proving that the score caused more revenue.

Keep the current policy and model version attached to each decision. Otherwise, a later review may compare outcomes across several routing changes while attributing everything to one new score.

A small pre-release test can expose a timing error without requiring a new model. Select one historical contact and write down:

Repeat for a contacted lead, an uncontacted lead, and an unresolved recent lead. These are diagnostic cases, not a representative performance sample. If the reconstruction cannot distinguish those paths, resolve the data-history problem before trusting a larger evaluation. A polished explanation cannot restore a feature snapshot that was never retained.

For each score release, retain the target definition, eligible population, feature timing assumptions, outcome window, evaluation period, routing action, capacity threshold, and known exclusions. Include the date and person responsible for reviewing business meaning.

Describe what changed from the previous version. A revised lifecycle policy may require a new evaluation even if the scoring formula barely changed. A new product or territory can create a population shift that historical averages do not capture.

Also define a stop condition. An unexplained drop in data completeness, a sudden score distribution change, or a mismatch between actual routing and documented policy should trigger investigation. A score should not remain authoritative just because it continues to produce numbers.

Review qualitative failures alongside aggregate metrics. A salesperson discovering that a high score came from machine-generated interaction is useful evidence about a signal problem. It is not proof that the entire model is worthless, but it should not disappear because the headline metric remains attractive.

There is another practical safeguard: retain a review route for records outside the highest-ranked queue. Without it, the organization can stop learning about the people its model consistently overlooks. The route might be a bounded manual audit, an approved exploration policy, or a segment-specific review, depending on the business and its obligations.

Do not call that review proof that every low-ranked lead deserves equal effort. It is a way to notice systematic blind spots and collect better evidence before making stronger allocation claims.

The review should have a defined sample, owner, and outcome taxonomy. Otherwise, a few memorable missed opportunities can dominate the discussion as easily as a flattering aggregate score. Both quantitative results and individual examples need a clear account of how they were selected.

The future of AI-assisted prioritization is not merely a more elaborate formula. It is a process that can distinguish what buyers did, what the company did, and what remains unknown.

A useful score can reduce wasted review time and make a team's reasoning more consistent. Those benefits still need verification in the actual workflow. They are not guaranteed by the presence of AI or by a strong historical correlation.

The question to take into the next scoring review is not only which leads converted. Ask which leads received a real opportunity to convert, what was known when they were prioritized, and whether the next policy will repeat the same blind spots.

That question turns scoring from a self-confirming ranking into a decision system the business can challenge and improve.

Campaigns Compete for the Same Inbox. Give Them a Shared Pressure Budget.

#9631. Why Most Online Personality Tests Hide Their Math (and How I Built a Client-Side 7 Deadly Sins Scorer)

If you have ever clicked a "free 3-minute personality test," answered 40 questions, and hit an email wall right before the result screen, you already know what is broken with most quiz sites on the web.

Even the ones that skip the paywall usually share two quieter design flaws:

When I built Vicefolk — a 21-question, browser-only 7 Deadly Sins self-reflection quiz — I decided to treat the scoring engine like a tiny open-source spec instead of a black box.

Here is how the math, the zero-backend friend-compare mode, and the client-side Canvas card exporter work under the hood.

The test uses 21 everyday behavioral statements — exactly 3 per dimension (pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath, sloth), interleaved so respondents aren't answering three Pride statements in a row.

Each item uses a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly disagree to 5 = Strongly agree). Every dimension is scored independently on a straight linear 0–100% scale:

Because each vice is an independent average of 3 integers (1..5), the possible scores sit cleanly on a 13-step grid (0, 8, 17, 25, 33, 42, 50, 58, 67, 75, 83, 92, 100).

We published the complete specification and test vectors under MIT on GitHub (seven-deadly-sins-scoring-spec) and wrote a plain-English results & tie-decoding guide explaining why multi-vice ties (like Pride 75% + Sloth 75%) happen frequently and shouldn't be swept under the rug.

We also label the whole project upfront as entertainment and self-reflection only — never clinical diagnosis.

Friends love comparing personality scores, which is normally the exact moment a quiz app forces both people to create an account and store their answers in a database.

Instead, we built Test With Friends around a tiny, strictly validated URL fragment (location.hash):

Why #compare=83.42.50.67.58.75.83 instead of a query string ?compare=...?

Most people share personality results as screenshots in group chats or Stories. Rather than spinning up a headless Puppeteer worker just to render result cards, the browser draws both a 1080×1350 (4:5) folio card and a 1080×1920 (9:16) Story card locally on after awaiting document.fonts.ready.

One subtle production bug we hit early: serving engraving illustrations from an image CDN without permissive CORS headers taints the canvas and causes canvas.toBlob() to throw a SecurityError at export time.

The fix was a tiny same-origin resolver that rewrites cross-origin asset paths to the site's same-origin /_a/ proxy first, falling back to img.crossOrigin = 'anonymous' only if needed, and caching Promise in a Map so switching card variants stays instant.

If you want to inspect the scoring behavior or test-drive the 3-minute quiz yourself:

#9630. How to Find and Fix JSON-LD Validation Errors: A Free Step-by-Step Guide

Structured data helps search engines understand the content, entities, and relationships on a website. However, even a small JSON-LD syntax error can prevent structured data from being interpreted correctly.

In this guide, we will explore common JSON-LD errors, how to identify them, and how to validate structured data using free online tools.

JSON-LD stands for JavaScript Object Notation for Linked Data. It is a widely used format for implementing Schema.org structured data on websites.

Developers can add JSON-LD inside an HTML script element without changing the visible page content.

This markup describes a website and provides its name and URL in a machine-readable format.

Validating structured data can help developers:

Valid structured data can help establish eligibility for supported rich results, but it does not guarantee higher rankings or rich result appearances.

A missing comma between properties can make an entire JSON object invalid.

Unlike JavaScript object literals, standard JSON does not allow trailing commas.

JSON requires double quotation marks around property names and string values.

Schema.org type names are case-sensitive.

Always check the official Schema.org vocabulary when selecting a structured data type.

Some structured data types require specific properties to qualify for Google rich results.

For example, a Product rich result has requirements that depend on the intended search feature.

A JSON-LD object can be syntactically valid while still failing a rich result eligibility check.

Always review the documentation for the specific search feature you are targeting.

There are several useful tools available for developers.

If you are developing structured data locally, you can validate the code before deploying it.

For larger websites, checking pages individually can become time-consuming.

Bulk URL checking can help developers review structured data across:

This is particularly useful after updating a shared layout, template, or structured data generator.

As part of the QBMFX Academy project, we have developed a free Schema Support Checker to help developers and website owners inspect structured data.

It is free to use and does not require account registration or a paid subscription.

Disclosure: I am associated with the development of the QBMFX project.

For a more complete structured data review, consider using these official resources as well:

These tools serve different purposes. Schema.org validation focuses on structured data vocabulary, while Google's Rich Results Test focuses on supported Google search features.

Developers can also use JavaScript to identify basic JSON syntax errors.

Remember that JSON.parse() checks JSON syntax only. It does not validate Schema.org vocabulary, semantic correctness, or rich result eligibility.

#9629. Does Fluoride In Drinking Water Affect Intelligence? What The Evidence Reveals

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, said:

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

Because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

#9628. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

Mermaid is the same shape: if (el.querySelector('.mermaid')), then import('mermaid'). The bundler emits each as its own chunk, and a document with no maths never requests KaTeX.

A side benefit: the first paint shows the text straight away. Equations and diagrams fill in a moment later, instead of everything waiting on the slowest library.

import hljs from 'highlight.js' pulls in every language it ships (190+). The fix is to import the core and register languages yourself:

Because each import() has a literal path, the bundler makes one small chunk per language. Then a loader that the highlighting pass awaits for every language the document's fences name:

The promise cache. A page with twenty JavaScript fences would otherwise start twenty imports of the same chunk. Caching the in-flight promise makes them share one.

#9625. Drone Photos to PLS-CADD: The Pipeline Behind a 161 kV Tower Twin

The job was a flood-damaged 161 kV transmission tower in Missouri, a circuit that could not be switched off, and a hospital on the same feed. The utility needed a recommendation, not a render, which set the bar for every step below. Here is the data pipeline we used, the parts that broke, and the choices I would repeat. We worked at night and on weekends, mostly because the utility's engineers were on the same schedule.

One flight produced about 700 images from a 45-megapixel camera, with position and orientation logged for every frame. The camera was a full-frame body on a gimbal, and those logs saved hours of alignment later. Five ground targets, measured with a total station, tied the set to real coordinates. The tower sits in a river bottom, so the ground was wet, the light was flat, and the deadline was measured in days. Flat light is fine for geometry and poor for texture, which matters more than it sounds when you are tracing steel against a grey sky. Photogrammetry settings that mattered

We shot 80 percent forward overlap and 60 percent side, then added a low ring around the base because the legs are close together and hide each other. The low ring was the difference between seeing the footing and guessing at it. Without the ground targets the cloud is a nice shape with no place in the world, and PLS-CADD will not accept a nice shape. Alignment ran in iTwin Capture, with the tower handled as a separate component so the tie to the existing line model stayed clean and reviewable.

Floodwater reflects and moves, and drone data from a wet site is full of traps. The mesher produced a surface that wobbled across the ponds and scattered stray points into the tower's lower panels. We masked the water in the photo set and rebuilt, losing a few frames to spray along the way. We also re-shot one panel the next morning when the water dropped. The base came out readable, which is where half the flood damage story lived.

iTwin Capture exported a reference cloud and an orthophoto. We traced member centerlines on the ortho, then checked every traced member against the cloud. The transmission tower went into PLS-CADD as a lattice structure with the adjacent spans and their tensions, and we re-checked the conductor data against the utility's records. Sizing a brace against the wrong tension wastes steel and time, so that check was not optional. We kept the tower body and the foundation as separate groups, because the tilt had to be reported at the base plate where the crew would work.

Tilt is not a number the photogrammetry tool hands you. We sliced the point cloud at two elevations, compared the centroids of each slice, and converted the horizontal offset to degrees. It is fifteen lines of Python, and it was the most-used code of the week because it was easy to defend in a review. Structural analysis starts with a number everyone can reproduce. We ran the function on five slices a meter apart to confirm the lean was consistent and not a local bulge in point density.

A single render hides the one member that moved. We computed the distance from each cloud point to the design surface and colored the result on a scale that capped at two centimeters. The map showed two bowed diagonals and a settled footing, which the field crew later confirmed. That geometric QA step became the before image for the repair, and it took minutes to regenerate after the second flight. The full-resolution map went to the utility; a downsampled version went into the briefing deck.

The cloud, the traced geometry, the PLS-CADD file, and the deviation map all got version stamps, plus a short note on what changed and why. When the braces were installed, we flew again and registered the new cloud to the old one. The comparison came out in centimeters, which is the only evidence that the repair did what the model promised. The digital twin we handed over is small enough to explain in a meeting and plain enough to survive a change of vendor. The folder structure is dated and flat, which sounds trivial until someone needs a file from last spring.

GenAnywhere converts a drawn polygon into building geometry plus a scene model of that area. We used it for the context around the line: the hospital block, the streets, the river edge. It never touches the tower model or the line loads, and I would not want it to. It is a context tool, and context is all we asked of it. The pipeline is not clever. It is short, repeatable, and it leaves a record that outlasts the storm.

#9624. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9622. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9619. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features
  • Limited to English language only
  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. #9617. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

Cover photo by Mark Weinberg; food styling by Liz Neily.

#9613. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9607. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9606. 3 Dark Personality Traits Linked To Infidelity

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.

The strongest average link is with psychopathy, closely followed by Machiavellianism.

Narcissism, which involves an inflated sense of self-importance and a need for admiration, has the weakest link.

Impulsivity, emotional coldness and a willingness to manipulate others may help explain why these characteristics are associated with betrayal.

The conclusions come from a review of 11 studies examining dark personality traits and infidelity.

Participants included university students, married couples and adults from the general population.

All three traits were positively associated with infidelity, although the strength of the association varied between studies.

Psychopathic traits include impulsivity, low empathy and a lack of guilt.

Someone with these characteristics may be more drawn to immediate sexual rewards and less concerned about hurting a partner.

A willingness to take risks could also make the possibility of being caught less of a deterrent — impulsivity and deception may help explain this link.

Psychopathy had the largest average correlation with cheating, although its association was close to that of Machiavellianism.

Machiavellianism involves a cynical view of others and a willingness to manipulate people for personal advantage.

In romantic relationships, these characteristics could make deception easier to justify when it serves someone’s interests.

However, a calculating approach may also encourage caution.

Someone concerned with protecting their reputation might weigh the potential rewards of an affair against the consequences of discovery.

This calculated approach could help explain Machiavellianism’s slightly weaker link with cheating.

Narcissism involves feelings of superiority, entitlement and a strong desire for admiration.

Attention from another potential partner may appeal to someone who places great importance on being desirable.

Nevertheless, narcissism had the smallest average association with infidelity and produced a less consistent pattern across the reviewed studies.

An inflated ego alone therefore offers relatively little information about whether someone has been unfaithful.

The broader picture may depend on how personality combines with relationship satisfaction, commitment and access to alternative partners.

Dark traits provide only part of the explanation for why people betray a partner’s trust.

The study was published in the journal Psihologija (Ataman & Yalçınkaya Alkar, 2025).

Yes, Thanksgiving is a pie-centric holiday. But what if you don’t like pie? Or maybe you just don’t want it. Either way, we’ve got lots of non-pie Thanksgiving desserts, from spiced pumpkin cupcakes to sugary apple cobblers, plus plenty of autumnal cakes.

This adorable cake pulls double duty, serving as both a scene-stealing centerpiece and a feast-ending dessert. To make, stack two mini Bundt cakes together and frost with orange buttercream. Carving this frosted pumpkin at the end of the meal may just upstage the turkey!

Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Mini Bundt Pan Set

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Clearjel

Cranberry sauce can be a polarizing side dish, but everyone will love this New England-inspired cake, which pairs tart cranberries with walnuts and vanilla for a simple, satisfying dessert. (Because it’s so quick to make, this is a particularly good recipe for any last-minute holiday baking.)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Sparkling Sugar

Sweet potatoes belong on the dessert table, and this recipe proves it. This ultra-soft cake is gently spiced and glows orange from the sweet potato purée, and it’s finished with a fluffy meringue that mimics marshmallow-topped sweet potato casseroles.

Instead of apple pie, try an apple pan dowdy on your Thanksgiving dessert table. The pan dowdy is a traditional American dish from the 1800s and early 1900s. A combination of pie and pudding, the name comes from the method in which the recipe is completed: After an apple-based filling is baked in a crust-lined casserole, the baker takes a fork and "dowdies" the crust, breaking it into pieces that remain crisp despite being partially immersed in the juicy filling.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" square pan

“Thanksgiving cheesecake” may not have quite the same ring as “Thanksgiving pie,” but when your guests are eating this ultra-creamy dessert, they won’t care. With its burnished top and custardy interior, this Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Boiled Cider
